10472-arthurian-chronicles-roman-de-brut:
Wace, a Norman poet, wrote the Roman de Brut in verse, translated here by Eugene Mason. The chronicle follows Geoffrey of Monmouth, whose Historia Regum Britanniae first united scattered Arthur legends into a lasting history. Wace, writing after Geoffrey, gave the story French verse form and wide fame.

About 1150, Geoffrey Gaimar had tried a French metrical chronicle, but Wace's Brut cast it into shade. Wace's gifts as poet and storyteller shaped Arthur's place in later annals. Readers get a key Arthurian source, in clear prose, for students of legend and medieval literature.
10856-a-narrative-of-the-siege-of-delhi-:
Charles John Griffiths, late captain of the 61st Regiment, wrote A Narrative of the Siege of Delhi. Henry John Yonge edited it, and John Murray published it in 1910, with plans and illustrations. The book opens at Ferozepore from May 10 to June 13, 1857: outbreak at Meerut, neglected arsenals, disaffection, and the 45th Native Infantry's failed attempt on the fort. Wives and families move to barracks as the cantonment burns.

Griffiths then follows the regiment to Delhi and the siege itself, from a soldier's view. His account criticizes commanders, praises troops, and records the mutiny's first shocks. Readers get a firsthand British narrative of 1857, detailed and partisan, as its officers remembered it.
11561-people-of-the-whirlpool-from-the-e:
Mabel Osgood Wright's 1903 novel is told from the experience book of a commuter's wife, opening on Candlemas with twins, a garden book, and a mild grey day. Letters from Miss Lavinia and Martin Cortright, a trip to town, and February violets follow in the early chapters.

As the whirl begins, families rearrange, gossip spreads, and a bug hunter joins the social round. The narrator's garden, her boys, and her neighbours give the book its shape, and the whirlpool of the title is the busy, talkative world just outside a suburban home.
14305-layamon-s-brut:
Layamon's Brut retells the chronicle of Britain's kings in vigorous early English verse, here in a readable modern rendering. Constantin the fair lands at Totnes with two thousand knights, summons brave men across the kingdom, and marches on London. Britons hiding in pits, woods, and fens like badgers pour out at his coming, women in men's clothes among them, thousands strong.

Arthur dominates the later narrative. Uther musters seven thousand chosen knights before, seven thousand thanes in the middle, and eighteen thousand behind, with footmen beyond counting, then marches to Meneve. Gillomar's men seize spears and battle-axes, breeches off, strange to see. Arthur demands peace with wisdom, reconciles the Danish king and his eldest son, and musters hosts from Norway, Denmark, Orkney, Moray, Galloway, Ireland, and Britain for France. Chronicle, legend, and battle poetry merge in a foundation text of English story.
144-the-voyage-out:
Rachel Vinrace sails to South America with her father and aunt, seeking a life beyond London drawing rooms. Virginia Woolf's Voyage Out, her first novel, follows Rachel among shipboard guests, a hotel colony, and a young writer named Terence Hewet. Talk, walks, and illness shape her growth.

Woolf experiments with free thought and shifting views while keeping a clear story line. Rachel's engagement to Terence promises a new life, but fever cuts it short. The novel's ending, quiet and stark, surprised early readers. It shows Woolf's voice forming before her great experiments.
14408-manners-and-conduct-in-school-and-:
The deans of girls in Chicago high schools wrote this 1921 guide to manners and conduct. It opens with maxims from Lincoln, Franklin, and Disraeli, and a verse from Spenser on gentle deeds. The book then gives plain rules for halls, classrooms, and streets. It speaks to schoolgirls who must learn how to behave in company. Its tone is firm, kindly, and old-fashioned.

In the assembly hall, pupils must not run, romp, or eat, and must take a seat at once and stay in it. Talk stays gentle, and singers gather in the center sections without being asked. A chapter on introductions warns against sloppy forms like Mrs. Jones, meet Miss Holbrook. Dance rules follow, down to the inches between partners and the place of each hand. The book drills courtesy as a habit, not a show.
16355-combed-out:
F. A. V.'s Combed Out, published in London by the Swarthmore Press in 1920, records a soldier's First World War in ten chapters. Squad drill opens the book, with a contemptuous sergeant teaching turns by common sense and exact obedience. The fatigue party, detachment, casualty clearing station, walking wounded, air raids, the German push, home on leave, across the ridges, and the armistice follow.

A Mark Twain epigraph on the national lie that supports tyrannies and shams sets the book's angry, honest tone. The author writes as a ranker, not an officer, about drill, wounds, and waiting. Readers of war memoirs will find a blunt, humane voice from the Western Front.
17412-the-bobbsey-twins-or-merry-days-in:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this first Bobbsey Twins book, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap, with the subtitle Merry Days Indoors and Out. The twins at home open the story, followed by rope jumping and what followed, the first snow storm, the broken window, and Bert's ghost. Coasting and what came of it, a snow house built by Freddie and Flossie, fun on the ice, and Freddie losing himself complete the early chapters.

Readers get a gentle family story of two sets of twins at play through the seasons, told in Hope's plain, kindly style. The book launched a series that kept children reading for decades. It suits young readers who enjoy everyday adventures, snow, and family fun.
17575-how-to-camp-out:
John M. Gould, author of a history of the First-Tenth-Twenty-Ninth Maine Regiment, wrote this guide to camping, first published in 1877, under the heading Hints for Camping and Walking. The contents open with getting ready, the first of many practical chapters for walkers and campers. Gould writes from experience, not from theory.

Readers learn how to choose ground, pitch camp, cook, walk, and stay safe outdoors, in the plain style of a veteran instructor. The book belongs to the early literature of American outdoor recreation, when camping was becoming a pastime rather than a necessity. It still reads as a sensible, old-fashioned manual for the woods.
1832-the-case-of-the-lamp-that-went-out:
Joseph Muller is no Holmes and no Lecoq: small, slight, plain-looking, and modest in manner, he solves his cases by patience and by noticing what louder men miss. Small, slight, and plain-looking, he works patiently and modestly, noticing what louder men miss.

The case turns on a lamp that went out and on a remark Muller himself recognizes as out of place, almost an impertinence, addressed to a man named Bormann. Groner builds the mystery from small social slips rather than from grand clues. The book is a good sample of the quieter European detective story, where character does the work of fingerprints.
18950-the-short-cut:
Jackson Gregory published this western novel in 1916, illustrated by Frank Tenney Johnson. The chapter titles trace a story of tragedy, suspicion, and pursuit: a homecoming, a gambler's bluff, a contemptuous rival named Sledge Hume, and a woman named Wanda whose discovery changes the game. A figure called Red Reckless and a promise made to little Saxon add to the tangle.

The action moves through ranch houses, town streets, and open country as old wrongs surface and new alliances form. Gregory builds his plot on secrets, grudges, and sudden reversals rather than on gunplay alone. Readers get a romantic western of the old magazine school, with strong heroines, proud villains, and a hero caught between duty and desire.
19501-the-boy-scout:
Richard Harding Davis wrote this story of a boy scout; its New York printing appeared in the mid nineteen teens with pictures. Jimmie, the hero of the frontispiece, drops a valise, straightens cramped fingers, and salutes, a small act that sums up the scout spirit.

Later a head clerk hides tickets in his waistcoat, trembling with excitement over a month-long boat trip in cabins called the Royal Suite. Davis's tale mixes city comedy with scout ideals: readiness, courtesy, and help given without fuss. A white-haired young man in a fast racing car tries to outrun the urge to do a stranger a good turn.
20104-the-cross-cut:
Courtney Ryley Cooper published The Cross-Cut in 1921, a western novel of mines and sudden death. Robert Fairchild finds an old man dead in a big armchair by the windows. A book lies on the worn carpet where it fell from slack hands. Fairchild picks it up and puts it back in the oak case.

That quiet, grim scene opens a tale of claims and cross-cut tunnels. Mining terms and greed shape the fights that follow underground. Cooper knew the West and its camps from his own reporting years. Readers get a tense tale where wealth in rock breeds risk above ground too.
23588-a-filbert-is-a-nut:
Rick Raphael wrote this science fiction tale, first printed in Astounding Science Fiction in November nineteen fifty nine. It opens with a joke that proves serious: the man in question was a nut, an institutionalised patient nutty enough to think he could build an atom bomb from modelling clay.

Miss Abercrombie, a manual therapist, pats old Mr. Lieberman on the shoulder and praises his finger painting. Patients work at long tables in a hospital arts and crafts shop, watched by bored attendants in spotless whites by a locked door. Raphael builds from that ward to a sharp, humane twist on madness, genius, and what counts as sane. Readers who like wry science fiction will enjoy the tale's blend of hospital detail and atomic dread.
2371-the-filigree-ball-being-a-full-and-:
Anna Katharine Green's Filigree Ball is a detective novel. A young woman is found dead at a ball, clutching a strange filigree ornament, and a lady detective must untangle the case. Green, a pioneer of American mystery fiction, builds the plot from clues, suspects, and a secret marriage, with her usual care for legal and domestic detail. The ballroom setting gives the murder its glitter.

The novel shows Green's gift for fair-play detection before the genre had rules. Its heroine detective was a novelty in her time. Mystery fans will enjoy a classic from the genre's early years.
23871-a-little-union-scout:
Joel Chandler Harris published A Little Union Scout in 1904, with pictures by George Gibbs. Its frame is a young lady, just returned from college, hunting her house for old things: furniture, china, and books. Her craze for the antique leads her to an old scrap-book her mother and the narrator thought safe under lock and key.

Reading it page by page in a sunny place, her curiosity wakes. The clippings tell of Civil War adventures. The illustrations catch their moments: Forrest shouting across a field, Whistling Jim running head down like a bull, and a leader with an evil-looking eye. Harris tells a Union scout's story through a daughter's discovery, with the war's melody wild and melancholy.
23924-kiddie-the-scout:
Robert Leighton published Kiddie the Scout in London in 1920, a continuation of Kiddie of the Camp, inscribed to Bernard Everett, who suggested it. Kiddie, a boy scout of the plains, faces a mysterious sniper, a dangerous enemy, and the sign of the broken feather.

Chapters follow lessons in tracking, a moonlight visitor, and Lone Wolf Cañon, with the cry of the jay and the ruse of the buffalo trail. Rube Carter's theory meets Kiddie's own, evidence mounts for the prosecution, and the battle of Poison Spider Creek settles matters. Leighton, who also wrote Rattlesnake Ranch and Cooee, gives young readers a Western scout story full of trails, clues, and pluck.
2484-the-boys-and-girls-plutarch-being-p:
Plutarch's Lives, retold for boys and girls, brings the great Greeks and Romans to young readers: Alexander and Caesar, Lycurgus and Numa, heroes and lawgivers whose choices shaped the ancient world. The retelling keeps Plutarch's moral focus, asking what made a life great or ruined it. The stories are short, vivid, and full of incident.

The volume served generations as a first history book, teaching character through example. Modern readers will find its heroes simplified but its stories still stirring. It remains a fine introduction to the classical world. The retelling pairs Greek and Roman lives, as Plutarch himself did.
24894-the-emperor-s-rout:
The Emperor's Rout, printed in London in 1831 by Charles Tilt with colored plates, is a verse frolic among the moths. The Emperor Moth is stung that the Butterfly's Ball was so splendid while moths were called too heavy to gallop and waltz. He vows to give a ball of his own and snub the pert butterflies.

Invitations go out to the Glory of Kent, the Belle of Brixton, the Peach-blossom, the Sphinx, Mother Shipton, and the Greek girls Lambda, Gamma, and Chi. Notes name each moth, from the Death's Head sphinx, feared as a messenger of pestilence, to hive-robbing hawkmoths. The book charms young readers who like bugs, balls, and rhyming natural history.
26631-a-virginia-scout:
Hugh Pendexter, author of Kings of the Missouri, published this frontier novel with Bobbs-Merrill at Indianapolis in 1922. He dedicates it to his son Faunce, his seven-year-old scout. The narrator, a surveyor and messenger between Fort Pitt and the Earl of Dunmore, shelters in a hollow sycamore eight feet across at the junction of the Monongahela and Cheat rivers.

Thirteen chapters carry three travelers over the mountains, through Indian-haters, a lost sister, Abb's Valley, and Dale's escape, toward peace in a clearing. The pack-horse-man's medicine grows stronger as shadows vanish and the Blue Wall is reached again. Pendexter fills the pre-Revolution border with loons, mockingbirds, honey-bees, and the constant question of whether settlement can hold.
27724-the-romance-of-a-mummy-and-egypt-t:
Théophile Gautier's Romance of a Mummy, translated and edited by F. C. de Sumichrast of Harvard, appears here as volume five of Gautier's works, published in New York in 1901. A companion piece on Egypt follows the novel.

The story opens with an English nobleman and a German scholar hoping to find an intact tomb in the Valley of the Kings, then unfolds the ancient tale of Tahoser. Gautier blends archaeology, romance, and lush description, and the volume shows French romantic fiction at its most pictorial. The Egypt section adds pieces on unwrapping a mummy, the road from Alexandria to Cairo, and ancient Egypt itself.
27750-admiral-farragut:
Captain A. T. Mahan's 1892 biography of Admiral David G. Farragut belongs to the Great Commanders series edited by James Grant Wilson. Mahan drew on the full biography by Farragut's son Loyall and on the admiral's journals and letters.

The book follows Farragut from his early naval service to his Civil War victories, including the capture of New Orleans and Mobile Bay. Mahan, himself a naval strategist, presents Farragut as the navy's most celebrated hero and explains the campaigns that made his name. A portrait and maps accompany the text, and the series also covered generals from Washington to Grant.
27824-juggernaut:
Alice Campbell's 1929 mystery Juggernaut opens in the south of France, where a young American woman named Esther seeks a position helping a local doctor. She rings the bell at Numéro 86, Route de Grasse, in February, with mimosa in bloom.

Inside the villa of Dr. Gregory Sartorius, Esther finds a household full of secrets and a manservant with a hostile stare. The novel builds its suspense from atmosphere, character, and the contrast between sunny Provence and the menace gathering indoors. Doubleday, Doran issued the book in its Front Page Mystery Series.
28315-one-way-out:
William Carleton wrote One Way Out in 1911 as the story of a middle-class New Englander who emigrates to America, in a wry, literal sense. Carleton, earning thirty dollars a week, finds middle-class life a kind of hell, and takes his family prospecting, labouring, and wintering in a new land. Chapters follow nine dollars a week, Sunday, plans, and citizenship.

From day labourer to fifteen dollars a week, Carleton learns the emigrant spirit first hand. His tone is frank, funny, and unsparing about class and work. The book offers a vivid record of an American who had to leave home to find America again.
28511-the-tree-that-saved-connecticut:
A school radio play by Henry Fisk Carlton, edited by Claire T. Zyve for Teachers College, Columbia University, The Tree That Saved Connecticut needs no costumes, scenery, or memorized lines. Players read from copies around a microphone, using voice alone to show feeling, with directions marking speakers as in, off, or coming in.

The cast includes Governor Treat, Lieutenant Allyn, Governor Andros, Captain Wadsworth, and Colonel Bligh. The play opens in 1661, when Charles II granted Connecticut a liberal charter of almost complete self-government. Its dramatic hours retell how colonists guarded that charter, in the story behind the famous tree.
29142-keep-out:
Frederic Brown wrote this short science fiction story about a Mars colony built on a single invention. With no room left on Earth and Mars hanging empty of life, planners hit on starting a colony there. Immigrants would change their habits and physical structure to fit the Red Planet, using a substance first called adaptine, then shortened to daptine.

The story is told by a colonist who learned the plan at ten, after landing in a glassite dome built for the children. Every factor was covered, the introduction says, except one flaw of human nature. Brown's twist turns on that flaw. Readers get a compact, ironic tale about adaptation, belonging, and the one human trait no plan can engineer away.
29381-the-works-of-charles-james-lever-a:
David Widger edited this index to the works of Charles James Lever, the Irish novelist who lived from 1806 to 1872. Rather than a novel, the volume maps Lever's books for Project Gutenberg readers, linking each title to its detailed chapter and illustration indexes. A word of explanation opens the guide.

Books indexed include The Confessions of Harry Lorrequer in full, Charles O'Malley, the Irish Dragoon, in two volumes, Lord Kilgobbin, and Cornelius O'Dowd upon men and women. Plate lists name engravings from Lorrequer, from the inn at Munich to the supper at Father Malachi's. Readers get a finding aid to a popular Victorian novelist, useful for navigating long, episodic novels chapter by chapter.
29562-the-clock-that-had-no-hands-and-ni:
Herbert Kaufman gathered twenty essays about advertising in this book, printed by George H. Doran Company in 1912, with copyrights from 1908 and 1912. The title essay tells of a clock that has no hands. A man who cannot track his own movements can no more win modern success with old methods than he can wear another age's shoes. Other essays include the cannon that modernized Japan and the tailor who paid too much.

Kaufman writes for business readers in brisk, aphoristic prose, praising new methods and mocking old ruts. Advertising, he argues, is a clock that must keep modern time. Students of marketing history will find a lively, period voice on selling in the age of the new century.
30036-word-study-and-english-grammar-a-p:
Frederick W. Hamilton, educational director of the United Typothetae of America, wrote Word Study and English Grammar as part six, number thirty-two, of the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices. The Committee on Education published it in Chicago in 1918. Its subtitle calls it a primer of information about words, their relations, and their uses, written for the young printer.

Hamilton argues that disregard of correct word use marks a man as inferior and bars business and social advance. A man's use of words, he says, is taken as a measure of his knowledge and even his intelligence. The contents run from word families, nouns, adjectives, articles, and verbs to pronouns, adverbs, prepositions, and conjunctions. Rules for correct writing, the sentence, the paragraph, common errors, tables of irregular verbs, and a glossary close a practical schoolbook.
3035-the-day-of-the-confederacy-a-chroni:
Nathaniel Stephenson wrote The Day of the Confederacy, volume thirty of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters follow the secession movement, the Davis government, and the fall of King Cotton. Reaction against Richmond, the critical year, life in the Confederacy, the turning of the tide, a game of chance, and desperate remedies follow. Stephenson writes from the southern side of the war. The book stresses that the Confederacy split into separate units as early as Farragut's capture of New Orleans.

Virginia, the two Carolinas, and Georgia formed the effective system while a detached western world fought alone. The narrative balances politics, economics, and daily life. It gives readers the companion to Stephenson's Union volume, compact and readable.
33392-in-and-out:
Edgar Franklin's In and Out, copyrighted in 1917, gathers comic tales of modern life, from the great unrecognized and theory's victim to opportunity, the reluctant one, and the wee small hours. Its chapters move through Johnson Boller proposing, the butterfly, scorned love, crime, the web, and the other lady, to a crash and a turn in the box. Franklin writes with a humorist's eye for social folly.

The book's frontispiece shows a girl of about a hundred and twenty pounds handled as a joke by Wilkins, a scene that sets its light, farcical tone. Its stories suit readers who enjoy period humor about love, business, and manners. For fans of early twentieth-century comedy, In and Out offers a brisk set of tales, each with a twist.
35180-sergeant-silk-the-prairie-scout:
Robert Leighton wrote a boys tale of a prairie scout named Sergeant Silk, issued in a cheap set of reward books at two shillings each. A front view shows Silk galloping off with a prisoner away from a brush fire, a scene from chapter four. Leighton had earlier written school tales praised in the same lists.

Chapter heads open with Silk looking like a destitute tramp, then a bag of gold and a puzzle in Grey Wolf Forest. A fugitive and his hunter, a night rider called Nick by Night, and a surprise visit follow in the early run. The set lists many like books for boys and girls at the same price.
35275-30-000-locked-out:
30,000 Locked Out, by James Beeks, was published at Chicago in 1887. The Gindele press printed the pamphlet history. Its subject is the great strike of the building trades there. Beeks frames the fight as one of individual liberty. That question, he writes, touches every industry and every class. Thirty thousand artisans and labourers stood affected, he says. Hundreds of employers and scores of dealers were hit too. Building stopped across the city. Capital of not less than twenty million dollars lay locked in vaults. The introduction grants the labour problem its real grievances.

Oppression has bound working people before, Beeks owns, and change came none too soon. But one class's wrongs, he argues, license no revenge from another. Exactions piled up, in his telling, until the unions themselves oppressed. The book pleads the employers' case.
3538-the-americanization-of-edward-bok-t:
Edward William Bok tells how a Dutch immigrant boy became one of America's most famous magazine editors in this autobiography. Bok, born in 1863, dedicates the book to his mother and his wife, the two women he credits most. He planned to write it in 1914, when he hoped to retire from editing The Ladies' Home Journal, but war delayed the work.

The story follows Bok from a poor immigrant home through newspaper offices to the editorship that shaped American homes. He writes about his own two personalities, the public editor and the private man, and about learning American ways without losing his past. The book won the Pulitzer Prize and suits readers who enjoy immigrant success stories and magazine history.
36196-boston-neighbours-in-town-and-out:
Boston Neighbours in Town and Out is a set of stories by Agnes Blake Poor, printed in eighteen ninety eight. Putnam's Sons published it in New York and London in that year. Eight tales fill the volume, several first printed in the Century Magazine. Our Tolstoi Club leads the set and sets its chatty, confiding tone.

The narrator lives in a Boston suburb she will only call Babyland in fun. Young married couples crowd it, and its sidewalks swarm with baby carriages daily. In winter the young folk are left to their own devices by the elders. A pouring rain keeps a party indoors one morning with nothing to do. Each guest must tell a story, and hers is the club's own tale. Other stories treat a little fool, a wall flower, and poor Ponsonby.
37458-natalie-a-garden-scout:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy wrote Natalie: A Garden Scout for A L Burt at New York in 1921, with the approval of the National Girl Scouts. Roy also wrote Janet: A Stock-Farm Scout and Norma: A Flower Scout. The Nourse Company held the copyright. A plate shows Natalie beginning her planting.

In an open letter Roy tells girls the incidents grew from her own girlhood. She trailed her father as he grafted fruit trees and hived bees, and shadowed her older brothers on hikes and fishing trips. Scouts were unheard of then, she says, yet the same stunts filled her days. Freckles, tan, and torn dresses earned her the name tomboy. Farm work and garden craft shape Natalie's tale.
39271-edward-hoare-m-a-a-record-of-his-l:
Edward Hoare is the life of a church man told from his own notes. Townsend shaped the life and set it out in London in 1896. A shot of Hoare stands at the front of the book in print. His own first words bless the sire and dam who raised him.

Boy days and school at Cambridge fill the first parts of the life. A turn of faith and the test for his rank come in their turn. A trip to Erin and the steps to the cloth fill the next stretch. His first posts, from a great town to a sea town, are traced in the book. The long years at his best known post fill the heart of the work. Work in far towns, home life, and trips fill the later parts. Sight lost and a last sick spell close the life of the man.
41260-dan-carter-cub-scout:
Mildred Wirt wrote this adventure for young readers, copyrighted in 1949, about Dan Carter and his fellow Cub Scouts. The book is dedicated to Paul Reinbolt, an assistant scout executive of the Toledo Area Council. Dan belongs to Den 2 of the Webster City Cub Scouts, led by Sam Hatfield.

The story opens on a rainy night in a riverside cabin. The den is camping on land behind the home of Midge Holloway's father, and the rain keeps falling on the tin roof. Hatfield wakes Dan to check the boat, fearing the river is rising. The chapter list points to trespassers, a trial for the Cubs, a rising creek, a crate of pheasants, and trouble on Rabb Island.
41279-the-butterfly-book-a-popular-guide:
Butterfly Book is a popular guide to the butterflies of North America. Holland, chancellor and museum director at Pittsburgh, wrote the guide. Doubleday, Page and Company issued this printing at Garden City in 1922. Rights pages date the core work to 1898 in its first form. Forty eight plates in colour photography show butterflies from his collection.

A front plate names spring kinds: Painted Lady, Hunter's Butterfly, Question Sign. Clouded Sulphur and Mourning Cloak join that bright first display. Text pictures present most kinds found in the United States. Holland held posts in learned societies of London and of France. Collectors and field walkers got a rich, plain guide to the tribe.
45083-the-library-of-work-and-play-mecha:
Fred Hodgson wrote a how to book for young workers, printed at Garden City in 1911 as one part of a childrens library of work and play. Sister volumes in the set cover carpentry, farming, home craft, and outdoor sports. A front photo shows a motor boat model, the kind of small job said to tax a young makers skill.

First lessons lay a cement path, with notes on digging, mixing, and moving heavy loads with lever and roller. Next comes the building of a boat house from an old barn, with blocks, ropes, and pulleys put to use. Bridge and boat work follows, with rules for a small launch and tips on docks.
4525-the-farm-that-won-t-wear-out:
Cyril G. Hopkins first published this farming book in serial form in The Country Gentleman, then issued it in book form after requests from farmers across the central, eastern, and southern states. His argument is plain: a farm need not wear out if its soil is fed and kept fertile year after year. Population growth, he says, makes the art of getting a good living from a small area of soil more valuable than ever.

Chapters take up permanent fertility, the nitrogen problem and its low-cost answer, phosphorus as the master key to lasting farming, and the link between soil care, profits, and future value. Hopkins quotes Lincoln and Liebig to stress that wealth lies in what the soil holds for plants, not in the land alone. Readers get a practical, hopeful manual for farmers who want land that keeps paying, rather than land that slowly fails.
45517-the-putnam-hall-cadets-or-good-tim:
The Putnam Hall Cadets, or Good Times in School and Out, is a school story by Arthur Winfield. Grosset and Dunlap of New York published it, with copyright in 1901. Winfield was the author of the Rover Boys series for boys. 

The contents promise the full round of cadet life at a military school. Early chapters introduce the cadets and send them to a rescue. A call on friends lands the chums in the hands of the enemy. A great game of football fills a chapter at the heart of the book. A circus visit brings a monkey and then a tiger on stage. The boys end as prisoners of a wild beast before the tale turns. A long march and further scrapes carry the story to its close.
45711-radiant-motherhood-a-book-for-thos:
Radiant Motherhood is a book for those who are creating the future, by the author of Married Love and Wise Parenthood. The author's other works listed include the Cretaceous Flora for the British Museum, a journal from Japan, and plays of old Japan. Her name stood on best sellers of the day, and this book shares their fire.

The contents begin with the young mother-to-be and her amazements. The young father-to-be and his amazements follow. Physical difficulties of the expectant mother get their own chapters of plain counsel. The book treats pregnancy as a state to be lived in health and joy, not endured in ignorance. It belongs with Wise Parenthood in its author's campaign to bring knowledge of the body to ordinary couples, in language a working mother could use.
46578-decorative-art-of-indian-tribes-of:
Frank Speck records craft in Decorative Art of Indian Tribes of Connecticut, a memoir of the Geological Survey of Canada, printed at Ottawa in 1915. The memoir is number 75 of the survey, number 10 of its anthropological series. The text rests on the edition of 1915.

The figures list the tools and the work. A Mohegan basket gauge and a hand splint planer lead the plates. Crooked knives with wood and antler handles and a bone punch follow. A typical basketry design of the Mohegans is shown in full. Mohegan and Niantic painted designs are set side by side for comparison. Field readers get a close record of the basketry and painted ornament of two Connecticut peoples, tool by tool and pattern by pattern.
47023-the-putnam-hall-champions-or-bound:
Arthur Winfield's school story, copyrighted in 1908 by Edward Stratemeyer and issued by Grosset and Dunlap, is the third volume of the Putnam Hall Series. The frontispiece shows the cadets packing away nearly every trophy the room contained.

Winfield's introduction says the series began when readers of his Rover Boys books asked what had happened at Putnam Hall before the Rover brothers arrived. The first volume told how the school was founded and followed Jack Ruddy, Pepper Ditmore, and their chums. This volume shows what the boys could do in contests on the lake, in the gymnasium, and elsewhere. The chapters promise a race on the lake, a gymnastic contest, a challenge from Pornell Academy, a bowling match, a great bicycle race, and a mystery of a bracelet.
475-in-darkest-england-and-the-way-out:
William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, sets out his plan to rescue the destitute of Victorian England, which he calls darkest England. Tales of hunger, drink, and homelessness frame a practical scheme. Booth borrowed Stanley's Darkest Africa title to shock readers about London poverty.

Booth proposes colonies, workshops, and farms where the poor could work their way back to honest life, under the Army's care. The book stirred wide debate, and it marks the moment when charity began to speak the language of social reform. His city colonies, farm colonies, and overseas colonies formed a ladder out of destitution.
47511-haiti-its-dawn-of-progress-after-y:
Haiti, its Dawn of Progress after Years in a Night of Revolution, is a travel and report book by Dryden Kuser. Badger published the book at Boston, copyrighted in 1921 by its author. A plate shows one of the main streets of Port au Prince at its front. Kuser dedicates the work to his wife Brooke, the source of his original interest in Haiti.

Contents open with Sargasso and Flying Fish, the sea road to the island in his telling. Cacos, the armed bands of the hills, and a bit of history follow in the chapters. Vaudoux, public education, and the president of the republic fill the middle of the list. Kuser wrote in the years of the American occupation of Haiti. His dawn of progress is the occupier hope for schools, roads, and order, set down by a sympathetic visitor of that moment.
49096-the-way-out:
The Way Out is a novel by Emerson Hough, published in New York in 1918. Hough dedicates it to James Alexander Burns, prophet of his people.

The novel is built in four books of chapters. Book one names the law and the gospel, a new creed, and a blood covenant. David Joslin awakens there, among the wandering women and a fabric of vision. Marcia Haddon and Polly Pendleton enter as chapters. Book two turns to the clans, the crossroads, and the original sin. The final chapter is the education of David Joslin. The opening scene is a cabin, where an old woman hushes Davy: he is coming.
49529-general-nelson-s-scout:
General Nelson's Scout, by Byron A Dunn, is a boys' novel of the Civil War in Kentucky, published at Chicago in 1898. Dunn dedicates the book to his little son Milton, who heard the story as it was written and gave many hints.

An opening essay sets the scene. Kentucky in 1861 tried to hold both North and South in her arms, and her heart, in the words of a noted son, burst in twain. Neutrality resolutions did nothing, and the state split into two hostile camps drifting toward the Confederacy. Then Lieutenant William Nelson of the navy, a popular Kentuckian, won leave to raise ten regiments for the Union. Hatred and opposition met him, even from Union men, but he never wavered. History and invention, Dunn warns, are closely woven in the tale that follows.
49950-papers-from-lilliput:
J B Priestley wrote Papers from Lilliput, a book of short gay essays. Bowes and Bowes issued the book at Cambridge in nineteen hundred twenty two. Priestley gives the set of trifles to his own father in its leaf. Some first saw print in the London Mercury and the Outlook.

More came week by week to the Yorkshire Observer’s wide crowd. There he wrote as Peter of Pomfret, a mask name for the task. On Filling in Forms and On Gossip head his list of small themes. An Apology for Bad Pianists pleads for the much blamed home player. On Getting Off to Sleep and On Travel by Train share the shelf. The Bogey of Space and A Mad Shepherd show his range of mood. On a Certain Provincial Player saves a dead actor from blank fame. Praise is the essayist’s last kind weapon, his first piece holds.
50451-a-boy-s-workshop-with-plans-and-de:
Boy's Workshop offers plans and designs for indoor and outdoor work for boys. Advertisements at the front of the hosted copy list special books for neighbourhood clubs. One series named is a reading union library for a young folks' union, at a dollar a volume. Its titles include tales of the great struggles for liberty and a romance of the sea.

Another advertised book gives the ways to success in business life. Eighty three business men answered the author's inquiries for it, the notice says. Volumes of lives of workers who won are listed next. Hints for living and young folks' histories by a well known author round out the list shown. The notices stress books as entertaining as stories yet educational in influence.
50685-the-story-of-genesis-and-exodus-an:
The Story of Genesis and Exodus is an early English poem of about the year twelve fifty. Richard Morris edited it for the Early English Text Society. The second and revised edition appeared in eighteen seventy-three, from Trubner of Ludgate Hill. The unique manuscript rests in the library of Corpus Christi College, Cambridge.

Morris's preface confesses he never saw the manuscript himself. F J Furnivall copied the text, and W W Skeat read the proofs against the original. The small vellum volume holds eighty-one leaves in a hand of about thirteen hundred. Every initial carries a dab of red. Genesis ends on the forty-ninth leaf and Exodus closes the book. Morris adds notes and a glossarial index. The poem retells the first two books of the Bible in the English of Henry the Third's reign.
51626-jacobean-furniture-and-english-sty:
Helen Churchill Candee wrote a guide to old English furniture in oak and walnut that Stokes of New York copyrighted in 1916. Forty three pictures go with the text. Her first chapter goes back to the wild days of American hunting for antiques. Every good piece was called Colonial, till a little learning sorted the kinds to their true classes.

The chapters walk the styles in order of reign. Early Jacobean work comes first, from the crowning of James the First in 1603. The pure Jacobean ends mid century. Then come the styles of Charles the Second and the Restoration. William and Mary close the century. The plates show great oak chests, gate leg tables, day beds, and spiral turned chairs. Candee writes for collectors who want to know what they own.
53197-cynthia-steps-out:
Cynthia Steps Out is a novel by Erick Berry, issued at Chicago in 1937. The contents chart a trip across Europe in eight chapters, each tied to a place. It begins on shipboard under the head Always Trust Your Luck, then moves to Paris. Brittany and Mont Saint Michel follow, then the Basque country and Carcassonne.

Siena and Venice close the route, in chapters called The Racing Snail and All Is Not Lost. The opening scene finds Cynthia, an artist, being fitted for a costume by her friend Stasia. Pins in her mouth, Stasia calls art fun, and Cynthia answers that she would not know how to be anything else. The ship tips as they work, and a pirate outfit is taking shape. Travel and dress up set the light tone at once.
53678-on-naval-timber-and-arboriculture-:
Patrick Matthew's On Naval Timber and Arboriculture was printed at London and Edinburgh in 1831. The preface is dated from Gourdie-Hill by Errol on September 10, 1830. Matthew admits he never read the classic planting authors, Evelyn, Hanbury, Marshall, Miller, and Pontey, and offers no apology. A writer, he says, does not obtrude like a speaker; the blame for wasted time lies with the reader. Critical notes on those authors form the book's subtitle.

Part one treats the structure of vessels: plank, timbers, and the figures of bends and crooks. Part two goes through the British forest trees suited for naval purposes. Oak leads, then Spanish chestnut, beech, the Scotch and English elms, willow, pine, and larch. The larch gets an inquiry into the causes of its rot and the soils where rot takes hold. Matthew mixes collateral matter through the technical argument to relieve its dryness.
54312-mons-anzac-and-kut:
An unnamed member of parliament wrote a war memoir in three parts, published at London in 1919 and dedicated to Lord Robert Cecil and the League of Nations. Mons covers August to September 1914. The author's regiment left Wellington Barracks at seven on August 12. He fell into step in the ranks and said goodbye to his brother at the gateway.

The streets were quiet, the papers having said nothing of troop movements. The men entrained for Southampton and sailed for Le Havre. French soldiers tumbled out to cheer them. Anzac treats 1915 and Kut 1916, giving the book its three battle names. The memoir joins a shelf of early first World War narratives.
61368-argonaut-and-juggernaut:
Argonaut and Juggernaut is a book of poems by Osbert Sitwell of London. Chatto and Windus issued the volume in nineteen nineteen after the war. Sitwell gives the book to the memory of Robert Ross, art critic. Some poems first ran in Wheels, the Times, and the Nation papers.

War verses at the end first appeared under the name Miles in print. The opening poem asks how we shall rise to greet the dawn. It calls for a new god of power, beauty, and strength to be made. The old god has made the Stock Exchange his temple, Sitwell charges. Young eyes, harnessed waves, and a torn paper moon fill the vision.
62386-melville-and-co-s-directory-and-ga:
Melville and Companys Directory and Gazetteer is a trade and place book for the towns of two east shires of England. This form was struck from a copy of the mid eighteen fifties, kept by a great town store of books. Its price to those who did not pledge in advance is set at its front.

Its towns run in a long row: Norwich and the old port by the sea, then Dereham, Swaffham, and a score more, great and small. A shore set of the next shire joins them: Ipswich, the abbey town, and Woodbridge. Each place gets a short tale of itself first, then its list: trades, firms, inns, and the chiefs of its church and town rule.
62426-black-out:
Black-Out, by Joseph Farrell, was produced from Planet Stories for winter 1943. A head line gives the stakes: the destiny of a dying world lay in another, a blue planet which could not control its own. The tale opens on Mars, with an old astronomer.

Old Thak watched fondly as the new telescope was put into its place. It duplicated one destroyed in the latest great war, and only Thak assurances had secured it. They were round bodied and young. Thak, the last astronomer of Mars, would teach them all he knew. Readers get a pulp tale of dying Mars watching Earth.
63988-last-night-out:
Lee Gregor tells a tale of two shipmates on shore leave in a story from Planet Stories for September 1951. Ensign Jed Grey and his blue-furred partner from Canopus walk the streets of Selby, Texas, the night before they ship out to war. Joe's true name is a soundless thought, so fleet records list him by number.

The town pours hostility at them, from Arcturians and Sirians but most of all from fellow earthmen in blue. Joe ranges his senses through the streets, hunting the feel of his own furred kind among a welter of strange thought. Grey, linked to his partner's mind, feels each wave of hate at first hand. Readers get a tense small tale of friendship across species, set in a port town the night before parting.
64874-space-blackout:
Space Blackout is a Mars tale by Sam Carson from the May nineteen forty one Comet. Jerry Kos, a star sail man of the Cosmic Survey, tells the tale in his own voice. He holds the lone run mark from Moon to Earth, set in twenty four thirty seven. His chief, Jim Drake of the ship Pelios, talks him into leave on Mars. Their host is Shadrak, a Mars lord who guards the Great Waterway there.

Mars men rule their world by robot craft and watch Earth from afar. They once crossed space to crush a Tartar tyrant and lift the United States. Shadrak shows the men a star sight room in his dome house. A dark cloud mass past Orion, named the Noir, draws his grave word. The tale turns on worlds that chose to die with their homes.
65456-life-of-james-mars-a-slave-born-an:
James Mars wrote his own life, a slave born and sold in Connecticut. The seventh edition came from a Hartford press in 1869. A certificate from Pittsfield stands at the front of the book. Deacon James Mars is known there as honest, upright, and truthful. He is an officer in his church, the paper attests.

Born a slave, the good providence of God has made him free, it says. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty, it adds. Mars wrote the story first at his sister's request, he tells. She lived in Africa thirty years, he says. She heard their parents tell of slavery. She was not born until years after they were free, though. When the late war began she wrote from Africa for the story. Mars gives the North a slavery of its own to remember.
65843-hideout:
Fox Holden wrote this science fiction story, printed in Imagination in May 1952. Its premise is a man with a price on his head who runs for his life, and who, when finally cornered, may have only one door left open to him: time.

The story opens aboard a pirate ship as a lookout reports an Earth merchantman, Marsbound. Captain Robbin Cutlass, angry and carrying a million-credit price on his head, orders his crew to track her down and fire torpedoes across her bow. He knows one ship cannot fight the whole space patrol alone. Readers get a space-pirate tale with a time twist held in reserve.
6636-hold-up-your-heads-girls-helps-for-:
Annie Ryder speaks straight to girls everywhere, with a title borrowed from Whittier's Primrose: hold up your heads, girls. Her chapters teach how to talk, how to know nature, how to make the most of work, what to study, and how to face moods and friends. School and home life both get practical, kind counsel.

Ryder opens with a craftsman's warning: one false stroke near the end can spoil a fine work, just as one careless act can mar a young life. Her tone is warm, not scolding, and her aim is steady character. Hold Up Your Heads, Girls is a charming 1886 conduct book, full of sense for young readers of any age.
66417-the-whole-truth-and-nothing-but:
Hedda Hopper and James Brough wrote The Whole Truth and Nothing But, a life put out at Garden City. Rights run from 1962 and 1963, held by Hopper in her name. She gives the book to her son Bill, with a jest on sass in both ways. She opens by a rule for books with such a bold name.

A life must start with the life of its teller, she says, and she starts with her birth. She was born to David and Margaret Furry, one of nine young ones in that home. Seven of the nine grew up, and three still lived at the time of the book. Her first home was Hollidaysburg, a fine town by Altoona in Pennsylvania. Her mother, whom she calls a saint on earth, named her Elda from a tale.
66888-a-merry-scout:
A Merry Scout, a children's book by Edna Payson Brett, was published by Rand McNally at Chicago in 1922. Riley drew its pictures. It holds four tales: the title story, Lending the Baby, Robert's Adventure, and Sandy's Valentine. A front picture shows Tilda and baby Maggie in her brand new coach.

Davy, the hero of the first tale, does not belong to any patrol and is not a real scout at all. It is not his fault: he is only nine and a half. That means two years and six months of waiting before he can wear the tenderfoot badge and go hiking like big Cousin Fred. Fred, sixteen, is a first class scout and patrol leader who holds the life saving badge. Davy swore the scout oath all by himself at his grandfather's farm. Brett writes of a boy scout in spirit.
6697-once-upon-a-time-in-connecticut:
Caroline Clifford Newton writes Connecticut history for the school children of the state, under the Colonial Dames of America. Yale's Charles Andrews oversaw the history, while friends, libraries, and the Connecticut Historical Society aided the work. The dedication speaks straight to young readers, as the book's true audience.

Tales of early Connecticut follow, told in a clear, story-like style that suits a classroom. The book aims to make state history feel like a tale, not a lesson. Once Upon a Time in Connecticut is a pleasant, old-style children's history, rooted in real places and people.
67053-janet-a-stock-farm-scout:
Lillian Elizabeth Roy, author of Natalie: A Garden Scout and the Blue Birds series, wrote this story for girls. The Burt Company published it at New York under a 1925 copyright, endorsed by the National Girl Scouts. It belongs to her Country Life series, where each heroine takes up a branch of farm work as a scout.

Janet Wardell rides the train to Four Corners one June Saturday. She reads the diary her friend Helene gave her the night before, with orders to record everything that happens at Green Hill Farm. Five girls will spend the summer there under a chaperone, and Janet means to keep tabs on the least thing they do. Fourteen chapters follow her arrival, trials at carpentry, tenderfoot scouts, poultry on strike, bees and bugs, and the fortune in keeping a cow.
67411-blotted-out:
Blotted Out, by Elisabeth Sanxay Holding, is a tale of a man who wants to vanish. A headnote calls Amy Ross a tigress in the shape of a fair woman, predatory and cruel. James Ross stands on a ship's deck in cold November rain, well content.

Ross has the windward side to himself, since no other passenger shares his taste for bleak weather. He is alone in the world, and he means to stay alone. Through the saloon window he can see a stern fellow passenger who boarded at San Juan. She has marked him down and means to give him her card before they land. A card would force one in return, and a trail to where he is going. Ross has dodged her so neatly that she cannot tell skill from chance.
67697-tales-from-a-dugout:
Arthur Guy Empey told tales from a dugout of the Great War's front. The book came out in New York in October 1918. Empey wrote Over the Top in his past war books. He gave this book to the folk who stay at home in war. The too old, the women, the unfit, and the young are named there.

Their hearts lie on France's fields while their flesh must stay, he writes. Seven men crew Gun Number Two of a gun troop in his start. Their gun is a Vickers, light, point three oh three in bore. Curly, a Scot, is named for one small curl he tends with care. Happy, a London man, helps him write his many notes home.
69767-all-about-miniature-plants-and-gar:
All About Miniature Plants and Gardens Indoors and Out is a handbook by Bernice Brilmayer. Doubleday published the book at Garden City in 1963. Sketches and garden plans by Fritz Schaefer fill the pages. Seventeen chapters run from window gardens to tiny bulbs.

Brilmayer had written matching guides to begonias and to vines. Here she treats gardens under false light, in glass, and in small greenhouses. Miniature roses get a chapter of their own, indoors and out. Sink gardens, rock gardens, and small pools follow in turn. Bonsai style trees and tiny shrubs close the plant lists. Colour plates show a garden planted in a wash boiler lid. The book served the postwar craze for small scale growing.
70391-martians-keep-out:
Fritz Leiber wrote a science fiction novelette that ran in a magazine in July and August 1950. It opens on a sign against Martians, with a black-shelled Martian body spiked beside the road as a grim warning. Hatred of the Martians, the head note says, was being worked up on purpose.

Scat, a scarred human, drives into the town of Bronsco with Click-Click, a Martian who speaks in pincer code. The town is shabby, its tall towers dead and its walks broken. Scatterday, as the note names him, must aid the Martians against human bondage, at risk of lynch law. Leiber makes bigotry itself the monster here.
71910-the-way-out:
The Way Out, a science fiction story by Richard R Smith, first appeared in Infinity for June 1958, with pictures by Richard Kluga. Its head note puts the stakes in one question: how do you kill a man without killing him. Unless that question can be answered, Earth will lose the war, and every Earthman will die. The tale is told from inside a prison of mirrors.

The captive cannot close his eyes; something has been done to them, and drugs ration his sleep. Hundreds of mirrors show him the nightmare shape of himself from every angle, and even his dreams carry the image laid over them. One relief remains: his right arm was left whole, so that if he gives in he can write the answers his captors want. They are clever with pain, he reflects, and patient.
74113-the-ice-goes-out:
The Ice Goes Out is a tale of Alaska by Frank Richardson Pierce. Its front line says that in it true men and crooks make plans, but strange Nature has the last word. The tale opens with the hand of the cold term on the north land. Sap has not yet run, and vale, stream, and peak lie as dead in the grip of the ice.

Then the sun swings north, and men take up talk of the ice pool. That pool, not the new year, marks the start of the north year. Men send coin with the day, hour, and tick they guess the ice will break. The man most near that tick wins the pot. One man pours his gold dust on a hut board and vows that this year he wins, past years of near loss. His mate asks if the we is meant.
74198-the-man-who-found-out:
The Man Who Found Out, by Roger Dee, was produced from Fantastic Universe for September 1954. A head note praises Dee fine, myth making name, and his flights of humorous scientific fantasy. The story own first line warns that it is one thing to blow a bubble of glib, journalistic lies.

It is quite another, the line goes on, to have that bubble burst in a nightmarish green beyond. The trouble with Fortenay was that he was not merely a skeptic, but a professional skeptic. He was a widely known, highly paid journalist. He had learned to profit from tearing down beliefs, and to spice his satire with wilful twisting of words. Fortenay serves aboard an ocean survey tug, the Cormorant. Readers get a tale where a debunker meets something he cannot talk away.
7436-the-development-of-religious-libert:
M. Louise Greene, who took her doctorate at Yale, traces how Connecticut moved from an established church to religious liberty. The monograph grew from three earlier essays. The first was a Yale thesis on church and state in Connecticut to 1818. The second was a popular article that won the Straus prize in 1896. The third was a paper honored by the American Historical Association in 1901.

The story runs from the colonial order, in which the Congregational church stood established by law, through dissent, taxation disputes, and the constitutional settlement of 1818. Greene argues that the past should teach the present, and that one generation can judge its own beliefs better by studying those of the last. The book is a careful state history with a national lesson about church and state.
74504-lucky-the-boy-scout:
Elmer Sherwood writes a boys' adventure in Lucky, the Boy Scout, printed at Racine, Wisconsin, with copyright in 1916. Alice Carsey draws the plates. The book is given to the Boy Scout who strives to live up to his pledge, as the gift page says.

Lucky meets John Dean at the start, and a fire soon tests the boys. The tale moves west to the Double X ranch, with cattle work and marsh folk. Train wreckers strike, and Ted is chosen for a mission to Chicago. A trap is set, a dictaphone does its work, and Ted wins a reward. The Marshes are joined again at the end.
74698-a-good-old-scout:
Theodore Seixas Solomons wrote the story A Good Old Scout as a test of sentiment between an old-timer and a newer prospector. A rich haul of gold is at stake, and the tale asks which man will drop his finer feelings and grab. Old Nock Whipple quotes scripture from his blankets on a tent floor.

The land flows with milk and money, Nock says, in a high, hopeful voice, though the berries must stew down for honey. McAdams tucks the old man's blankets back and tells him he talks too much, then cuts stove wood. A third man writes in a diary in the corner. Fall has painted the arctic highland, and winter nears. Gold camp manners fill the tale.
78710-in-doors-and-out:
In Doors and Out, or Views from the Chimney Corner, gathers the sketches William Adams wrote as Oliver Optic. Lee and Shepard of Boston issued the new edition in 1875, twenty-one years after the first, and Adams re-dedicated it to his old friend Charles Kimball, sheriff of Middlesex.

Many pieces first ran in the Boston True Flag, the American Union and Gleason's Pictorial. Adams calls them home thrusts at the follies of the parlor and the kitchen, the shop and the counting-room. Titles include Getting an Indorser, Six Hundred a Year, The New Minister, Family Jars and Life Insurance. One love story was dropped for this edition, and new pictures were made.
8467-frost-s-laws-and-by-laws-of-america:
Frost's Laws and By-Laws of American Society promises a condensed but thorough treatise on etiquette and its usages in America, with plain and reliable directions for deportment in every situation in life. Subjects include letters of introduction, salutes and salutations, calls, conversation, invitations, dinner company, balls, morning and evening parties, visiting, and street etiquette.

S. A. Frost's manual served a rising middle class eager to behave correctly, and its plain directions show what counted as polite in Gilded Age America. Readers today get both a rule book and social history: riding and driving, travelling, and table manners as a system. The book's thoroughness is its charm, and its window onto manners.
9295-a-night-out:
Edward Peple wrote this comic tale in which the hero is a cat, Omar Ben Sufi, a splendid tiger-marked Persian of purest breed. Omar's pedigree runs to Padisha Zim Yuki Yowsi Zind, and his tail rivals Solomon in all his glory. To laymen he was just a cat, dwelling with an exclusive family in an eighty-thousand-dollar cottage near town.

A night out sends Omar into scrapes that wound his aristocratic pride and test his languor. Peple writes with arch humor, letting the cat's dignity carry the jest. The book is a light, charming fancy for animal lovers and humor readers alike.
a-narrative-of-the-siege-of-delhi-with-a: Charles John Griffiths, late captain of the 61st Regiment, recounts the siege of Delhi and the mutiny at Ferozepore in 1857, edited by fellow officer Henry John Yonge. The narrative opens at Ferozepore in May, with the outbreak at Meerut, neglected arsenals, and the first signs of disaffection among native troops, before following the regiment toward Delhi. Plans and illustrations accompany a soldier's view of confused orders, repulsed attacks, and a cantonment set alight.
a-night-out: Edward Peple builds this comic tale around Omar Ben Sufi, a splendid tiger-marked Persian cat who regards himself as aristocracy. He traces his pedigree to a long line of dignified ancestors. Living with an exclusive family in a costly cottage near town, the cat enjoys a pampered life among selected weekend guests. The humour lies in the gap between his lofty self-image and the plain fact that to most readers he was simply a cat.
arthurian-chronicles-roman-de-brut: Wace, in translation, retells the Brut chronicle of British kings from Brutus to Arthur and beyond, drawing on Geoffrey of Monmouth. The verse history won wide favor in its age, and French and British chroniclers used it as an authority for later annals. Its blend of legend, battle, and court life fixed Arthur in chronicle form for centuries. Readers meet a world where history and romance walk side by side.
britannica-1911-bahut:
Bahut, a French word of unknown origin, names a portable coffer or chest. Its lid is rounded and covered in leather garnished with nails. People used it to carry clothes and personal luggage. In short, it was the original portmanteau, or travel trunk. Mentioned as early as the 14th century, its form survives in the modern trunk.

Some bahuts were richly ornamented or divided into compartments inside, but all stayed readily portable. The name fell out of use toward the end of the 1600s. Coffer replaced it in ordinary speech. That loss explains why French romantic writers of the early 1800s misused bahut. They applied it to almost any old buffet or wardrobe. In building, the same word means a plain low wall that carries a church roof, hidden behind the balustrade.
britannica-1911-bakhmut:
Bakhmut is a town of Russia in Ekaterinoslav government. It stands near the river of its name, 136 miles east of Ekaterinoslav city. Salt springs gave the town its origin. Their discovery came late in the 1600s. Settlements grew around those briny wells.

The town counted 19,416 people in 1897. Coal comes from its ground today. Salt remains a leading product too. Alabaster and quicksilver join the list of minerals. Steel rails are manufactured in its works. Springs, mines, and rail works make its record. Few town entries in this volume run shorter. The facts given are origin, place, people, and products. Nothing is said of buildings or history. That silence itself shows a purely industrial place.
britannica-1911-barring-out:
Barring-out was a school custom, once common in England, in which pupils shut their master out of the school, as explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At Bromfield school in Cumberland, the boys deposed and excluded the master for three days at the start of Lent, a practice said to go back beyond memory. The doors were barricaded, and the boys armed themselves with mock weapons to hold the building.

Terms ended the siege. If the master forced his way back in, the boys took extra tasks as a penalty and did them willingly. On the third day a surrender was signed, often in Latin verse, and it always won the boys football and a cockfight at once. The custom lasted long at Eton, the entry notes, and turns up in many school stories.
britannica-1911-betel-nut:
Betel nut is the name of a fruit chewed across much of the East. The 1911 Britannica entry warns that the name betel covers two plants. One is the Areca palm, which bears the nut itself as its fruit. The other is a vine whose leaf is used with the nut. That vine is kin to the plant that yields black pepper.

The palm is native to the Malay lands and the isles near them. Growers plant it wide, from south India and Ceylon to Siam. It is a slim tree with a straight, bare stem of great height. A crown of six to nine large fronds tops the trunk. The fruit is the size of a small hen's egg.
britannica-1911-bristol-connecticut:
Bristol is a township in Hartford county, Connecticut, in the central part of the state about 16 miles south-west of Hartford. It covers 27 square miles and holds the village of Forestville and the borough of Bristol, incorporated in 1893, both on the Pequabuck river. Counts give 7382 people in 1890, 9643 in 1900 and 13,502 in 1910.

Clock making is the borough's fame: Bristol clocks, first made soon after the War of Independence, have long been widely known. Woollen goods, iron castings, hardware, brass ware, silver plate and bells fill out its factory list. First settled about 1727 as part of Farmington, the place formed its first church in 1742. An Episcopal church followed in 1748 whose members leaned Loyalist in the Revolution; their rector was tarred and feathered by Whigs, and member Moses Dunbar was hanged for treason.
britannica-1911-brut:
Brut, also called Brute or Brutus the Trojan, is a legendary British figure treated in this short 1911 Britannica entry. According to Geoffrey of Monmouth and other writers, he was the hero from whom Britain took its name.

The legend made him a grandson of Aeneas who was banished from Italy, made his way to Britain, and founded New Troy, the city later known as London. The entry explains the name as a confusion between Bryt, meaning a Briton, and the classical name Brutus. For the romance literature built on the story, readers are pointed to the articles on Wace and on John Barbour.
britannica-1911-camping-out: Camping out is the sport of cast off house life to live in tents, vans, or boats. It grew in full craft in new times, and a vast shelf of books has been writ on it. Past a short note that names that fact, the piece is a guide list of those books by part of the world. Lists cover Europe, the south lands, and the great land past the west sea. Works on camp gear, camp cook craft, and wood craft all find a place.
britannica-1911-cashew-nut:
Cashew Nut is the subject of a nature article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The cashew nut is the fruit of a tree native to the West Indian Islands. The fruit is shaped like a kidney and is about an inch long. Its kernel sits inside two coverings. The outer covering is smooth, grey, and leathery. A dark layer inside holds a sharp, biting juice.

The article says the kernels taste mild, oily, and pleasant. People in warm lands eat them raw and roasted. They also yield a light sweet oil said to match olive oil for cooking. Below the fruit, the stalk swells into a pear shape with a tart taste. That part is eaten as the cashew apple. It can be brewed into a drink and then distilled. The tree stem also yields a gum like gum arabic.
britannica-1911-chingleput:
Chingleput is a town and district of British India, in the Madras presidency. The town stands thirty six miles by rail from Madras city. Its people numbered ten thousand five hundred fifty one in nineteen o one. With a town in North Arcot, Chingleput was once a capital of Vijayanagar kings. Those kings took that role after their fall at Talikota in fifteen sixty five.

In sixteen thirty nine a local chief granted land to the East India Company. Fort Saint George now stands on that granted land near Madras. The old fort at Chingleput held a key place, ringed by swamp and a lake. The French took it in seventeen fifty one, and Clive retook it a year later. In later wars it gave refuge to British troops and local people. The town is noted for pottery and trades in rice.
britannica-1911-conneaut:
Conneaut is a city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city in Ashtabula County, Ohio. It stands on Lake Erie at the mouth of Conneaut Creek, some sixty-eight miles north-east of Cleveland. Its people grew fast: 3,241 in 1890, 7,133 in 1900, and 8,319 in 1910. Three rail lines serve it, and car ferries cross the lake to Canada.

The city lies in a grain and dairy district and has a fine harbour. Coal and ore move through that harbour, and the city is a sub-port of entry. Its works include planing mills, flour mills, brick works, and plants for lamps and light fittings. The city owns and runs its own electric light plant. Surveyors built a log storehouse on the site in 1796, and lasting settlement dates from 1798.
britannica-1911-enfield-connecticut:
Enfield, a township of Hartford county, Connecticut, is the subject of an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the north of the state, on the east bank of the Connecticut river. It has an area of thirty five square miles and three villages, Thompsonville, Hazardville, and Enfield. The census of 1910 gave it 9,719 people.

Its chief goods are gunpowder, carpets, brick, cotton press machinery, and coffin hardware, and much tobacco is grown nearby. Enfield was first settled in 1679 as part of Springfield, Massachusetts. It became a separate township in 1683 and part of Connecticut in 1749. In July 1774 its town meeting voted that a firm union of the colonies was vital for civil rights. It also called for a halt to all trade with Britain until the tax acts were repealed. A Shaker community settled in the township in 1781.
britannica-1911-gamut:
Gamut is a music article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the full range of notes a voice or instrument can make. The word joins gamma, a Greek letter used as a music sign, to ut, the first syllable of a medieval hymn. In its strict, older sense, a gamut is the scale of an age. Its roots lie in the medieval great scale.

That scale was long credited to Guido of Arezzo, of the eleventh century. The article says the credit fits better with Hucbald, who died in 930. In his scheme, scales were built of four-note groups. The half step always fell between the second and third notes of the group. Later, a note was added below the group and one above it.
britannica-1911-gout:
Gout is the subject of a medical entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry calls it a disorder of the whole body that shows itself in swollen joints. At times it leaves deposits of salts in the joints. It can also bring changes in key organs of the body.

The text traces the name through French to the Latin word for a drop. That name reflects an old view that bad matter dropped from the blood into the joints. Greek doctors of old knew and described the ailment under varied terms. The entry notes that those old terms were used for both gout and kindred joint pains, which makes the early record hard to sort.
britannica-1911-isabella-of-hainaut:
Isabella of Hainaut, queen of France, gets a short royal life in the 1911 Britannica. Born at Lille in eleven seventy, she was the child of Count Baldwin the Fifth of Hainaut. Her mother was the sister of Philip of Alsace. She wed King Philip Augustus and brought the land of Artois as her dowry. She was crowned at Saint Denis in eleven eighty. Scribes of the day saw the match as a join of two great royal lines.

Philip did not hold her dear, the text says in plain terms. In war with Flanders he sought to put her aside at a court at Sens. His uncle spoke for her and saved the match. She died in childbirth in eleven ninety. Her son went on to reign as King Louis the Eighth of France.
britannica-1911-juggernaut:
Juggernaut is a worn form of the Sanskrit Jagannātha, Lord of the World, the name under which the Hindu god Vishnu is worshipped at Puri in Orissa. The legend holds that the sacred blue stone image was first worshipped in jungle solitude by an outcast mountaineer named Basu. King Indradyumna of Malwa sent Brahmans out in all directions until Basu was found.

The image was then taken to Puri, where a temple begun in 1174 was finished fourteen years later at a cost of over half a million pounds. The present temple is a pyramid 192 feet high, crowned with the wheel and flag of Vishnu. Its walled yard, near 400 feet by 300, holds many small shrines. The main shrine holds three rough wooden images: Vishnu, his brother, and his sister. Daily rites run all year, and four meals a day are served to the images.
britannica-1911-meerut:
Meerut, a city, district, and division of British India, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The city stands halfway between the Ganges and the Jumna rivers, 37 miles north-east of Delhi. Its people numbered 118,129 in 1901. The city proper lies south of the military quarters.

The article traces a fall and a rise. The place reaches back to the days of the Buddhist emperor Asoka, but its modern weight came from its choice as a great British military station. In 1805 it was named a ruined town of few people. The cantonment was set up in 1806, and the count of people climbed fast in the decades after. The town is a chief centre of the cotton trade. It was here, the entry notes, that the first outbreak of the Mutiny of 1857 took place.
britannica-1911-middletown-connecticut:
Middletown is a place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It describes a city in Connecticut in the United States, on the west bank of a large river. The city is the seat of its county and lies south of Hartford. Steam boats, rail lines, and electric lines all serve the town.

The entry gives counts for three census years and lists the chief schools. A large university founded in eighteen thirty one stands on its main street. A church school and a free public library are also named. Stone quarries across the river and town factories add to its wealth. The town owns and runs its own water works.
britannica-1911-milford-connecticut:
Milford, a township of New Haven county in Connecticut, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies on Long Island Sound, about ten miles south west of New Haven. The Housatonic river parts it from Stratford on the west. Its area runs to about sixteen square miles, and its count reached 4366 in 1910.

Rail and electric lines link Milford with Bridgeport and New Haven. A chain of liked beaches lines its shore, among them Woodmont, Pond Point, and Walnut Beach. The Wepowaug river crosses the town and flows into the Sound there. Milford keeps the stamp of an old New England town. Many of its steady folk descend from the first settlers. Its burial ground holds the tomb of Robert Treat, a leader in King Philip War.
britannica-1911-moreton-bay-chestnut:
Moreton Bay Chestnut is a tree entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Moreton Bay chestnut is a tall tree of Queensland and New South Wales. Its botanical name is Castanospermum australe, and it belongs to the pea family. The entry gives the marks by which the tree and its fruit are known.

Its pods are almost round in section, about nine inches long and two inches broad. A spongy layer inside divides each pod into three to five cells. Each cell holds one large seed shaped much like a chestnut. The native people roast and eat these seeds. The timber draws a second notice: it looks somewhat like walnut. It is soft and fine grained and takes a good polish. Against those virtues the entry sets one fault, for the wood is not durable. Readers get a short, practical portrait of an Australian tree.
britannica-1911-norwalk-connecticut:
Norwalk, a city of Fairfield county in Connecticut, is described in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the Norwalk river, in the town of the same name. It sits by the side of South Norwalk and west of Bridgeport. Its count rose to six thousand nine hundred and forty five in nineteen ten.

Rail, tram lines, and steam boats link it to New York. The city has a green with old churches and fine elms. It holds a free book house, a ward for the sick, and a state drill hall. A group of women of the town set up a drink font in the name of Nathan Hale. Hale took his guise as a Dutch school man in this town. He then set out on the spy trip that cost him his life. Mills make cloth and more in the town.
britannica-1911-norwich-connecticut:
Norwich is a city in Connecticut in the United States, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets out. It is one of the county seats of New London county, in the township of Norwich. It stands where the Yantic and Shetucket rivers join to form the Thames. Its count in 1910 was 20,367 for the city and 28,219 for the township.

Rail lines, steamers from New York and New London, and electric lines link Norwich to its neighbours. It is the head of navigation on the Thames, whose channel is 100 to 200 feet wide and 14 feet deep. The older, residential part of the city stands on rising ground between the valleys of the two streams. The business district lies along their banks below that ground.
britannica-1911-philippa-of-hainaut:
Philippa of Hainaut, queen of Edward the Third of England, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. She lived from about 1314 to 1369. Her father was William the Good, count of Holland and Hainaut. Her mother came of the royal house of France.

Edward visited her father's court in 1326 with his mother Isabella. Philippa was wed by proxy at Valenciennes in October 1327. She landed in England that December and married Edward at York in January. Her marriage portion was seized by the dowager queen. The alliance still paid, winning Edward troops and support from her kin. Those allies stood by him in his French wars that followed. At home she planted a colony of Flemish weavers at Norwich. She also pushed coal mining on her Tynedale estates.
britannica-1911-salzkammergut:
Salzkammergut is the subject of a district entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is a district of Austria in the south west of Upper Austria, between Salzburg and Styria. It forms a separate imperial domain of about two hundred fifty square miles. Its fine scenery earned it the title of the Austrian Switzerland.

Its name means salt exchequer property, and its wealth rests on salt mines. That origin is stressed in the entry from the start. The district belongs to the Eastern Alps and holds the Dachstein group. The most easterly glaciers of the Alps lie in that group. Peaks and ice fields are both described in detail.
britannica-1911-timor-laut:
Timor Laut is a group of islands in the Malay Archipelago, described in an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group lies south-west of the Aru Islands and was held by the Dutch, who split it into the districts of Larat and Sera. Yamdena is the largest island, at about 1,100 square miles.

The entry describes low, flat coral islands, one volcanic islet with a dead crater, and the sole safe roadstead at Ritabel. It lists buffalo, a cuscus, bats, and rare birds among the wildlife. The people, put at about 19,000, are described as Papuans mixed with Malay stock, noted for a strong sense of art.
britannica-1911-torrington-connecticut:
Torrington is a borough in Litchfield County, Connecticut. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces it from mast swamp to mill town. It stands on the Naugatuck River west of Hartford. Its people near doubled between 1900 and 1910 counts.

A public library from 1865 held fifteen thousand books in 1909. A state armoury also stands in the borough. Mills made it a rich making center by 1905. Factory goods that year topped nine and a half million dollars. Pine woods first covered the town site in 1734. Ships yards prized those pines for masts, hence Mast Swamp. A wool mill built by the Wolcott family in 1813 spurred growth. The village took the Torrington name only in 1881.
britannica-1911-walnut:
Walnut, a group of trees in the genus Juglans, is explained in a plant entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. About ten species make up the group. They grow in mild lands of the northern half of the world, reaching into Mexico and the tropics of South America. All are trees, most of them large.

Leaves grow in turns along the stem and split into uneven leaflets. The trees hold a sharp, resin rich juice. Leaf scars are large and stand out clear. More than one bud can form in a leaf axil, a useful trait. If frost kills the first shoot, a spare bud grows in its place. Male flowers hang in thick catkins from the prior years wood. Female flowers stand alone or in small groups on new growth. The fruit is a kind of drupe with a fleshy husk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-beirut:
Beirut, in Phoenicia, is a titular Latin see and the residential see of several Oriental prelates. Its earliest form was likely Beeroth, springs, and Berytos probably comes from Berûti, a fish-goddess's Phoenician name. Birthplace of the early Phoenician author Sanchoniathon, it seems unimportant in remote times. After Antiochus IV Epiphanes it was called Laodicea of Chanaan until Alexander Zabinas (129-123 BC).

Strabo says Tryphon destroyed it, yet its coin series runs complete from 123 to 14 BC, so it was quickly rebuilt. Rome enlarged it, garrisoned it with two legions, and made it the colony Julia Augusta Felix Berytus in 14 BC. Herod the Great and both Agrippas built sumptuous monuments there and gave gladiatorial combats.
