Its missionaries remain Catholicism's strongest bulwark in Syria, served by a precious documents collection begun at Paris in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-connecticut:
James Henry Webb's entry surveys Connecticut, five thousand square miles. It ranked among the thirteen colonies declaring independence in 1776, early to ratify the Constitution, under which the republic took present form in 1789. The 1900 census counted 908,420 people, passing one million by 1908, growth in cities while rural towns held on. Manufacturing, not farming or commerce, formed the principal resource.

Plymouth traders founded the first English settlement at Windsor in 1633. Dutch traders raised a house and fort upriver. Windsor, Hartford, and Wethersfield united on 24 January 1639 under a first constitution. Connecticut ceded public lands in 1786, reserving some three and a half million Ohio acres, and adopted its present constitution in 1818. Religious polity runs through the entry. Puritan planters framed the 1639 constitution. Sunday observance stood strictly by law, blasphemy statutes dated from settlement, and Assembly sessions opened with prayer and chaplains. Statutes regulated church societies and incorporation, while confessional communications carried no legal privilege.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-greyso:
A biographical entry follows Daniel Greysolon, Sieur du Lhut, the French explorer who gave Duluth its name. Born near Saint-Germain-Laval about 1640 and dead at Montreal in 1710, he served in the French army, fought at Senef in 1674, and sailed for Canada that same year.

From Montreal he pushed west in 1678. He took possession of the Sioux country for France in 1679. He explored Lake Superior and the high plateau where the Mississippi, Red, and Saint Lawrence rivers rise. He built Kaministiquia, now Fort William, and Fort La Tourette on Lake Nepigon. First Canadian to explore the West, he rescued Father Hennepin from captivity and laid the foundation of Detroit in 1686.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-father-prout:
Father Prout was the pen name of Francis Sylvester Mahony, Irish priest and writer. Born at Cork in 1804, he studied at Clongowes and in France. Ordained at Lucca in 1832 against his superiors' advice, he served in Cork. During the cholera epidemic he worked heroically as a hospital chaplain.

Moving to London in 1834, Mahony began writing for Fraser's Magazine. Dickens later posted him to Rome for the Daily News. His Reliques of Father Prout mix erudition, fancy, and sharp and caustic wit. Best known for The Bells of Shandon, he died in Paris in 1866.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-cabassut:
Jean Cabassut, a French Oratorian theologian born at Aix in 1604 and dead there in 1685, joined learning to holiness and a ready charity. He entered the Oratory at twenty-one, taught canon law at Avignon, and spent eighteen months at Rome with Cardinal Grimaldi, archbishop of Aix.

Back home Cabassut wrote on church history, canon law, and moral theology, and Saint Alphonsus counted him a classic. His Notice of Councils, enlarged in 1680 into a collated history of councils and canons, long served as an authority under the name Cabassutius. His canon law theory and practice ran through many editions across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-amadeu:
Johann Amadeus Franz de Paula Thugut, an Austrian statesman born at Linz in 1736 and died at Vienna in 1818. He was a paymaster's son called Franz through life, despite the baptismal Johann Amadeus. Tales of Maria Theresa finding him abandoned are myths; she schooled him at the new Oriental academy for his father's service.

Thugut entered imperial service in 1754 as translator at Constantinople, won Kaunitz's praise, and became state chancery secretary. All the while he secretly drawing thirteen thousand livres a year from Louis XV, a pension he kept as embassy secretary from 1769. Raised to lower nobility in 1771, he later persuaded the Turks on Bukovina and steered Austrian policy through revolution and war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kharput:
Kharput, Armenian Kharpert, meaning 'rocky fortress', is an Armenian Catholic diocese founded in 1850 in eastern Anatolia. This entry describes a very old hill city, built under the first Armenian kings, whose ruined fortress, tower, and walls still stand at about 4,350 feet.

Height and scarce water are pushing residents down to Mezre, three miles away on the plain. Kharput still holds 30,000 people and serves as capital of the newly created province (vilayet) of Mamouret-ul-Aziz. The diocese counts 3,000 faithful, eight parishes, six churches, three chapels, 14 stations, and 14 primary schools. Some 72,000 Christians live among about 600,000 people in the whole province. An American Protestant mission, large and based at Kharput, heads all such missions in Armenia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michael-wolge:
Michael Wolgemut, a painter and engraver, was born at Nuremberg in 1434 and died there in 1519. He stood as Nuremberg's foremost fifteenth-century artist, picked to paint the great altarpiece at Zwickau. Hans Pleydenwurff had him as pupil and helper; Wolgemut took over his master's technique with care, though he must not be ranked his equal. His surest claim to lasting fame is that Durer learned from him, working alongside him from 1486 to 1490.

In those years his workshop counted among the city's busiest, crowded, Dodgson notes, by the best painters, carvers, and wood engravers of the day. Whether Wolgemut cut wood himself is still unsettled, but many carved wooden altarpieces came out of his shop, and Veit Stoss, the famed carver, was his friend and workmate. He plainly made some woodcuts, and designs for several Nuremberg stained-glass windows are his. His chief picture after the Zwickau one hangs at Crailsheim.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-denaut:
Pierre Denaut was the tenth Bishop of Quebec, born at Montreal on 20 July 1743. Schooled at Montreal and Quebec, he was ordained in 1767 and made pastor of Soulanges at only twenty-four. During the American invasion of 1775 he kept his flock faithful to their sovereign. Transferred to Longueuil in 1787 and made vicar-general in 1791, he became coadjutor to Bishop Hubert and was consecrated on 29 June 1795.

He stayed at Longueuil after succeeding to Quebec in 1797, governing chiefly with Bishop Plessis. He visited his whole diocese, crossing Upper Canada to Detroit in 1801 and 1802. In 1803, via Burlington and Boston, he reached the Maritime Provinces, where Acadians and Indians saw a bishop for the first time. He founded Nicolet College in 1803 and helped enlarge Montreal College in 1804. He resisted a British governor's claim to present to parishes and the Royal Institution's Protestant control of instruction. He died at Longueuil in 1806.
combed-out:
Combed Out, by F. A. V., was published by the Swarthmore Press of London in 1920. A transcriber's note gives the initials a name: Fritz August Voigt, who chose to be called Frederick. Ten chapters follow one conscript through the Great War, from Squad Drill to The Armistice. A Mark Twain sentence stands at the front, aimed at the silent, colossal national lie.

The first sergeant teaches turns on heel and toe in broad dialect. Later chapters take in fatigues, a casualty clearing station, air raids, the German push of 1918, and home leave. German prisoners at a waiting room door answer his questions with relief: all glad to be out of it, no more fighting for them, Gott sei Dank.
doe-osti-2997324-an-assessment-of-the-er:
Benjamin Reedlunn, Seth King, Brad Day, and co-authors size an error inside the safety case for the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant, in Sandia report SAND2025-12225 dated September 2025. WIPP stores transuranic waste in deep salt beds in New Mexico. Its performance assessment needs rock porosity over time to judge brine and spalling releases, but fully coupled rock-and-fluid simulation is too slow to run.

Assessors instead read porosity from a prebuilt response surface, a look-up table keyed to time and fluid pressure. That shortcut fails when a pressure history strays from the ones used to build the table, because real rock response depends on the path taken. The team ran 600 representative pressure histories through both the table and the full mechanical model and compared porosities. The spread gives regulators an honest error band for the shortcut.
doe-osti-3007880-a-north-carolina-retros:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory letter report ORNL/LTR-2025/4149, by Hillary Fishler and Supriya Chinthavali, looks back at major power outage events across North Carolina counties from 2020 to 2024. The tool behind the analysis is TASTI-GRID, which compiles outage records county by county.

Hurricane Helene in September 2024 swamped the state's records: Buncombe County, home to Asheville, logged 91 major outage events that year, over 500 percent more than second-place Yancey County's 15. Yet Buncombe and Mecklenburg counties already topped the outage counts in 2020 to 2023, with 34 and 27 events, before any hurricane arrived. The pattern points to standing resilience problems that storms magnify.
doe-osti-3007891-cleap-project-or-sage-a:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/SPR-2025/4179, by Femi Omitaomu and Brandon Miller, dated September 2025, applies the OR-SAGE siting tool to Montana, Utah, and Colorado for the CLEAP project. OR-SAGE screens land parcel by parcel against the requirements of energy facilities. Separate chapters treat each state with the same screening method.

For data centres, dropping the cooling water requirement changed the Montana map sharply: 32 counties passed 50 percent suitability, and 8 of those reached 90 percent or more. Reservation land still removed most of Roosevelt and Big Horn counties from play. The state chapters let planners see where power, cooling, land, and fibre lines actually line up.
doe-osti-3009942-reticular-materials-and:
Final technical report for DOE award DE-SC0024500 covers mining valuable metals from seawater with reticular materials. These are metal-organic frameworks built like molecular scaffolding. Francesco Paesani of UC San Diego led the work, with Tod Pascal and Omar Yaghi of UC Berkeley. The period ran from September 2023 to August 2025.

Simulations and synthesis centred on MOF-808. Its large pores treat lithium, sodium, and potassium almost alike, about minus 4.1 kilocalories per mole each. The small pores decide selectivity, and water flips the answer: into a dry small pore, potassium wins at about minus 7.4 kilocalories per mole and lithium faces the highest entry barrier. Into a wet small pore, lithium becomes the most stable ion.
doe-osti-3023487-participation-in-intens:
Pavel Snopok of the Illinois Institute of Technology closes out award DE-SC0019264, covering May 2023 through September 2025, with this report on intensity frontier neutrino physics. His program office contact work sat inside Fermilab's flagship NOvA experiment, which together with Japan's T2K pursues sharper values for neutrino mixing. Open questions include whether neutrino masses follow a normal or inverted ordering and which octant the mixing angle θ23 falls in.

Group members also worked on beam instrumentation, where a halo around the beam spot was adding stray hits and cutting live time early in each spill. One researcher coordinated using the test-beam detector as a profile monitor, installed scintillator paddles to characterize the halo, and ran beam studies with line physicists. Firmware updates with larger buffers then raised live time and trigger rates.
doe-osti-3030267-bull-trout-and-westslop:
Brian J. Bellgraph of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and partners from Eastern Washington University, the Kalispel Tribe, and the Army Corps of Engineers tracked two trout species below Albeni Falls Dam. Bull Trout and Westslope Cutthroat Trout have declined in the Pend Oreille Basin, partly because hydropower dams cut their habitat into pieces. Radio tracking ran from September 2008 to July 2010, following 10 adult Bull Trout and 17 adult Westslope Cutthroat Trout in the dam tailrace.

Both species roamed widely, shifting between spillway and powerhouse zones. In spring flood season they gathered at the left powerhouse zone, close to the dam concrete. In quieter seasons they searched across the tailrace. The pattern points to a fishway entrance near the left powerhouse as the best build site, a finding meant to guide passage design at the dam.
doe-osti-3366851-potential-applications-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory survey LA-UR-26-24592, version 0.3.0, maps where quantum computing could serve the laboratory's missions. Nineteen authors, led by Andreas Bärtschi, Francesco Caravelli, and Carleton Coffrin, map candidate applications across the lab's physics, chemistry, and computing programs. The August 2025 volume is a planning document: where might a quantum device beat the classical supercomputers Los Alamos already runs?

Workflows get concrete treatment. A materials study, for example, derives a Fermi-Hubbard model, fixes filling and temperature, then studies phases and conductivity; a quantum kernel could replace the hardest step, ground-state estimation or thermal sampling. Similar mappings cover other simulation and optimization problems. The report's value is triage: it separates plausible near-term uses from speculation, with references for each claim.
doe-osti-3484507-energy-storage-siting-a:
Pacific Northwest workshop report, dated May 2026, by Devyn Powell and Jessica Kerby, sums up outreach on siting and permitting energy storage. Battery projects often stall on local permits, not technology. The workshop gathered the people who face those stalls.

Cited research in the pages covers battery cost paths and rural electric storage guides. A national rural cooperative guide from 2020 is among the sources. Discussion themes run from safety worries to permit timelines. Developers and local officials get shared ground for storage talks, with sources they can check after the meeting ends.
frost-s-laws-and-by-laws-of-american-soc:
Frost compiled this guide to American manners for the fashionable world. She promises plain rules for every social situation. Chapters cover calls, introductions, and dinner company. Balls, parties, and visiting get detailed treatment. Street conduct, travel, and church behavior follow. Weddings, baptisms, and funerals each have their place.

The rules are short and direct. A gentleman gives the upper side of the pavement to a lady. No one pushes through a crowd or crosses a funeral line. Dress, letter-writing, and card tables are also governed. One hundred extra laws handle odd occasions. Frost drew on English, French, and American authorities. The book shows what polite America expected in 1869.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAUnitedAutoWo:
The headline carries the whole story of a 1967 embarrassment: Ex-Agent Says Victor Made Request; Reuther Concedes UAW Got CIA Funds. Frank C. Porter reported for the Washington Post on the United Auto Workers' turn in the great CIA funding scandal.

When the agency's secret subsidies to private organizations broke into print, labor's turn came. An ex-agent said Victor Reuther had requested the money, and Walter Reuther conceded the union had received CIA funds for its international work. The article is one clipping from the avalanche that ended the CIA's covert funding of American civic life. It is preserved as it ran.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RayJerryAbout_R: FBI agents interviewed Jerry William Ray on April 29, 1968, three weeks after the King assassination. Jerry Ray was James Earl Ray's brother, and agents questioned the family hard in the manhunt's last weeks. An interview record fixes the date, the place in the inquiry, and the man's own statements as agents wrote them down. The file gives the interview's date and subject. It does not summarize Jerry Ray's answers, so they cannot be described here.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_Ins: Able Archer 83 was a NATO exercise in November 1983 that rehearsed the release of nuclear weapons. Soviet leaders, fearing the drill might mask a real attack, put their own forces on alert. This briefing-book page presents the record of that war game and the scare around it. Its title says the episode put United States-Soviet relations on a hair trigger. The evidence here is the title alone, but the event is now widely treated as one of the Cold War's most dangerous misunderstandings.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico-a: Keeping the Secrets: US Silence about Ayotzinapa - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
hold-up-your-heads-girls-helps-for-girls:
Annie H. Ryder's Hold Up Your Heads, Girls! offers practical help for girls in school and out of it. Ryder borrows her title from Whittier's Primrose, who told her daughters that handsome conduct, not looks, is what counts. She dedicates the book to her girls everywhere.

Chapters advise on how to talk, how to get acquainted with nature, and how to make the most of work. They also discuss what to study, and how English literature and other studies fit a young woman's education. Later chapters treat moods, womanliness, friendship and the relations of youths and maidens, always in a direct, encouraging tone. The book speaks to readers who want a period picture of how a thoughtful Victorian author counselled girls toward confident, useful lives.
how-to-camp-out:
John M Gould wrote this camping manual, first published in 1877. Gould had written a Maine regiment's history, and he writes like a soldier. Small parties afoot and large parties with baggage wagons get separate chapters. Clothing, stoves, cooking, marching, and camp craft follow in order.

Tent making is taught with a draftsman's care. An A-tent is laid out on the floor, line by line, in drilling cloth. Edward Everett Hale adds a chapter of his own, and Dr Elliott Coues adds hygiene notes. A diary chapter shows the art in use. Soldiers and boys of the day got a complete, thrifty school for the woods.
in-darkest-england-and-the-way-out:
General William Booth, founder of the Salvation Army, published In Darkest England and the Way Out in 1890 as a plan to rescue Britain's poorest. Part one, The Darkness, counts what Booth called the submerged tenth: the homeless, the out-of-work, drunkards, criminals, and children of the lost. He piles up cases and figures from London streets.

Part two, Deliverance, lays out his scheme in detail. City colonies would feed and employ men, farm colonies retrain them, and a colony overseas would settle them abroad. Rescue homes, a prison-gate brigade, a poor man's bank, and a poor man's lawyer complete the design. Booth wrote as an organizer raising an army, not a bystander.
layamon-s-brut:
Layamon's Brut is an early English poem retelling Britain's legendary history. The hosted sample opens in the thick of battle and march. Constantin the Fair lands at Totnes with all his host.

Two thousand knights march with him toward London. The Britons hide in pits, woods, heaths, and fens to escape. Messengers summon every brave man in the kingdom to court. Layamon wrote in English soon after the Norman age. His poem preserves old British tales in a rough, powerful early verse. Arthur stands at the center of Layamon's long chronicle. Battles and kings pass in a stately, drum-like rhythm.
manners-and-conduct-in-school-and-out:
Manners and Conduct in School and Out was written by the deans of girls in Chicago high schools. Allyn and Bacon published it, copyrighted in 1921 by Fanny R. Smith. A line from Spenser opens it: the gentle mind is known by gentle deeds. Maxims from Lincoln, Franklin, and Disraeli follow.

The book teaches schoolgirls how to act in class and beyond it. Lessons cover speech, dress, honesty, and respect for others. Its sayings urge that whatever is worth doing is worth doing well. Time, warns Franklin, is the stuff life is made of. Such manuals shaped American school manners for a generation. This one speaks with the voice of women educators.
nasa-tm-19690017085-manned-space-station:
Robert R. Gilruth, director of the Manned Spacecraft Center, presented this speech in San Antonio on June 25, 1968. He spoke at the Fourth International Symposium on Bioastronautics and the Exploration of Space. His theme is the manned space station as gateway to our future in space. That old dream of engineers, he argues, is newly practical.

Three developments clarified the picture, Gilruth says. The Saturn V rocket now provides a major building block for station design. Knowledge of the living and working environment crews need has also grown greatly. Station science programs, studied in depth, now define real use requirements. He closes with present Apollo Applications plans and speculations on future orbital stations.
once-upon-a-time-in-connecticut:
Caroline Clifford Newton wrote these tales of early Connecticut. The Colonial Dames of Connecticut sponsored the book. They dedicated it to the school children of the state. Professor Charles Andrews of Yale supervised its history. Libraries and the state historical society helped prepare it.

The introduction praises Connecticut's quiet, steady colonial life. Towns were scattered, rural, and largely self-governing, it says. Roads were poor and travel slow between settlements. Town meetings handled local affairs for ordinary people. The colony shaped men and forms of government, it argues. Children gain a love of their local past here.
people-of-the-whirlpool-from-the-experie:
Mabel Osgood Wright called People of the Whirlpool the experience book of a commuter's wife, and dated it 1903. It takes the form of a journal, opening on February 2, Candlemas, in mild gray weather. The writer jokes that if the woodchuck ventures out and sees no shadow, winter owes them a rebate.

The contents promise twins, Miss Lavinia's letters to Barbara, Martin Cortright's letters, and Barbara's trips to town. The whirlpool is New York society, pulling at a household trying to live in the country. Wright mixes nature notes, gossip, and letters into a commuter-age comedy of manners.
the-americanization-of-edward-bok-the-au:
Edward William Bok, whose dates are given as 1863 to 1930, tells his own life in The Americanization of Edward Bok, subtitled the autobiography of a Dutch boy fifty years after. He dedicates the account to his mother and his wife. One gave him birth and raised him, he says; the other blessed him with home and family.

Bok explains that the book was planned for 1914, when he meant to retire from active editorship, but war brought new duties and set it aside. He chose then to write of himself in the third person. That distance, he says, let him watch the public editor Bok at work, praising and blaming him as if he were another man.
the-bobbsey-twins-or-merry-days-indoors-: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Bobbsey Twins, or Merry Days Indoors and Out, the first book of her long set. Grosset and Dunlap of New York put it out, with rights dated 1904 from the Mershon Company. The first parts place the twins at home, then take up rope jumping and what came of it. The First Snow Storm, The Broken Window, and Bert's Ghost follow. Coasting, and What Came of It is the last part named. A plate shows two sleds sweeping down a long hill.
the-boy-scout:
Richard Harding Davis wrote The Boy Scout, put out in New York by Charles Scribner's Sons in 1914. The tale opens with the scout rule: each day, do some one a good turn. Davis is clear on the spirit of it. The turn is not done since the copy-books say a kind act earns one back. A true scout, till the act is done, has a dark day.

Once the turn is proved, the scout may face the world with a clear mind and untie the knot in his scarf. Jimmie Reeder unties that knot at ten past eight on a hot August morning. His good turn was to give one dime to his sister Sadie. With it she could go to a show, and the plate shows Jimmie, valise dropped, pulling his cramped fingers straight to salute. Small stakes, warmly told, set the tale's tone.
the-boys-and-girls-plutarch-being-parts-: The Boys' and Girls' Plutarch holds parts of the Lives of Plutarch, edited for boys and girls by John S. White. The list starts with Theseus and Romulus, set side by side, then Lycurgus and Solon. Themistocles, Camillus, Pericles, Demosthenes, and Cicero follow. Alcibiades and Coriolanus are paired, as are Aristides with Cimon. Pompey, Alexander the Great, and The Death of Caesar stand in the list too. Short pieces are cut from other lives, among them the engines of Archimedes and a portrait of Cleopatra.
the-case-of-the-lamp-that-went-out:
The Case of the Lamp That Went Out, by Augusta Groner, translated by Grace Isabel Colbron, begins with the same introduction to Joe Muller used across the Muller volumes. Muller, of the Imperial Austrian secret service, is small, slight, and plain, with none of Sherlock Holmes's authority or Monsieur Lecoq's brilliancy.

His humility has causes. A wrongful imprisonment in his youth left a stigma. It shut him out of honest work until the police took him. The bureaucracy of his department keeps his rank low. Yet kings and councillors consult him. He asks no honours, only an income for his simple needs and the chance to work at what he most enjoys. The detective is fully drawn before his case is allowed to start.
the-day-of-the-confederacy-a-chronicle-o: Nathaniel W. The subtitle calls it a chronicle of the embattled South. Its contents begin with the secession movement, the Davis government, the fall of King Cotton, and reaction against Richmond. the-development-of-religious-liberty-in-:
M. Louise Greene, PhD, explains in a preface that her monograph on religious liberty in Connecticut grew from three earlier, shorter essays. The first, Church and State in Connecticut to 1818, was her doctor's thesis at Yale. The second won the Straus prize offered in 1896 through Brown University by the Hon. Oscar S. Straus, and the third took honorable mention in the Justin Winsor prize competition of 1901.

Connecticut's path, she argues, was not marked by wild disorder, cruel oppression, class tyranny, or civil war. Its contribution was a pattern of stability and reason in government, slowly broadening the idea of liberty as restrictions on religious and personal freedom softened. Yet New England is recalled as a hard place for those who were not Congregationalists, and she hopes a fairer judgment of colonial men and measures will follow.
the-farm-that-won-t-wear-out:
Cyril G. Hopkins wrote The Farm That Won't Wear Out first as a series in The Country Gentleman, then as a book at the call of farmers in many states. Words from Lincoln and from Liebig head the work.

Hopkins asks what makes soil stay rich for good. His chapters take up what crops take out of land, the puzzle of nitrogen and its cheap fix, and phosphorus, which he calls the master key to lasting farming. He ties soil wealth to farm profit and land value. The aim is plain: feed the soil so a farm can feed folk for good.
the-filigree-ball-being-a-full-and-true-:
Anna Katharine Green wrote The Filigree Ball as a mystery in three books, from The Forbidden Room to The House of Doom. A full and true account of a crime's solution is promised on the title line.

The first book opens with talk of the Moore house, a signed name, Veronica, and gossip at work. The second book turns to law and its victim, with thrust and parry in court. The third moves south to Tampa and a colonel's own men, seeking the heart of the puzzle. Green builds her case from small clues, house secrets, and a ball where a fine chain holds the key.
